Thank you very much, Madam Minister. I think the point that you made is leadership. makes a difference. And I think we are looking to the similar kind of leadership from the SIDS as well. And our next speaker is from the minister from Jamaica, Minister Samuda. I've listened to you yesterday morning very eloquently on governance aspects of it, and given what your two predecessors had said, would welcome your views on the subject.

Thank you, sir moderator, Ambassador Thompson, Excellencies, colleagues. The ocean is one connected system. Our governance should reflect that reality. Over the past 50 years, we have developed an extensive international architecture for its governance. UNCLOS, BBNJ agreement, we have the UNFCCC, we have the Convention on Biological Diversity, the IMO, Regional Fisheries Management Organizations, and of course, the International Seabed Authority, and several other processes. Jamaica has a particular connection to this architecture. We know that Kingston is the home of the International Seabed Authority. Jamaica has also ratified the BBNJ Agreement, which entered into force earlier this year. Each of these institutions and agreements indeed have an important mandate, but from the perspective of Jamaica, and I believe many other SIDS, the difficulty often arises from the point of implementation. Our communities do not experience climate change separately from biodiversity loss. officials do not experience ocean warming separately from changes in marine ecosystems and fish stocks. And our governments cannot effectively address coastal resilience separately from food security, tourism, infrastructure, and economic development. Yet the international system often asks us to respond to these interconnected issues through separate processes, separate reporting requirements, and separate financing mechanisms. This is one of the disconnects I believe we must address. Jamaica therefore posits that the answer is not necessarily another institution, but rather stronger coordination among the institutions we already have. And this is where we believe the UN system can continue to add greater value. Firstly, we need greater coherence at the level of national implementation. In Jamaica, we use National Coastal and Oceans, National Council on Oceans and Coastal Zone Management, where we bring all institutions together. We suggest that this is a route that should be followed by other nations. Secondly, we should reduce the administrative burden on SIDS and harmonize the process of reporting across the varying processes. Thirdly, and this is an issue that affects all SIDS and indeed developing nations, need greater coherence in finance. A mangrove restoration program, for example, can deliver climate adaptation, biodiversity protection, and coastal resilience, but our financing architecture must become better at recognizing and financing these multiple benefits. Finally, the SG can use its convening authority to bring these systems together in ways that individual treaties and institutions cannot readily do on their own. As such, Jamaica would therefore support stronger practical coordination across the UN system, focused on implementation rather than creating another bureaucracy and negotiating process. And to be fair, we do see that in work package 27, that there is some coherence coming, but we support stronger and urgent action. We also invite all of you here after Canada to join us in 2029 at the Our Oceans Conference. I believe if we were designing international ocean architecture afresh, it would start with the ocean rather than the institutions. We would recognize from the outset that climate, biodiversity, fisheries, development, and human security are indeed interconnected. It is the reality in which we live. Thank you.

Our next speaker is from a country that has put the ocean agenda on the United Nations calendar in a manner of speaking with going all the way back to Ambassador Oud Pardo. We have now Ambassador Simone Borg, Ambassador for Climate Action from Malta. You have the floor, Madam.

Thank you very much. Thank you very much. It's a great honor and pleasure to be here. And I wish to salute everybody, especially distinguished heads of government, ambassador, and distinguished colleagues. I will be brief. I will try and list about seven solutions which I think could work. First of all, I think it's understanding the context where we work with, in the sense that we will work within the international legal framework that is We do not have a centralized lawmaking body. It's made by states, implemented by states at the national level. So there is that discretion and also the lack of compulsory jurisdiction. And I think understanding that these are the sort of the shortcomings of the system will help us to find the solutions in a better manner. And I definitely want to link this with what my colleague from Brazil has just said about the need, therefore, for the muti-approach, for the involvement of non-state actors to fill in the gaps gaps and to keep the momentum going because this is, after all, a way how the non-state actors participate in improving the legal framework itself. And we have some, also, some good examples, like MARPOL's Annex 6, for example, or the Fish Stocks Agreement that refers to the RFMO rules as the applicable conservation measures. So we have this kind of linkages, even sometimes between treaties. Sorry, I think I'm going a bit fast for translation. Okay, sorry about that. So those are examples we can look at and perhaps follow and try and find better examples. The second solution, I would say, would be literacy, understanding what we, as much as possible, that the message reaches all stakeholders, that the need for a holistic approach to you know, to protect our ocean, empowering stakeholders to endorse this approach, because we all know that the ocean is subject to various interests, conflicting interests. And until we have this kind of literacy that we are, after all, protecting the ocean that gives us all the sustenance and all the resources that we need. If the ocean fails, if it dies out, we will lose everything. So I think this kind of mentality of protecting the ocean from a holistic manner needs to reach the literacy message. Also, literacy in the sense that lawmaking must be linked to science. That is the paradigm shift, I think, that we have had from the past. We have norms that are centuries old, but they were never based on science. And it is only when the science inspired lawmaking that we started having this holistic approach towards protecting the ocean. Another possible solution is what some other speakers have already mentioned, the need to formalize cooperation and coordination, particularly perhaps among executive secretaries of treaties, not necessarily creating another institution, but not leaving it to chance or to one-off examples. And we also need to also show this opportunity that we're working together. Then you have also the need to address skills gaps because a holistic approach needs to change that mentality. as well as identifying crucial contributors, which are the partners as the port states, the coastal states, the flag states, the role, how they can improve this holistic approach. Last but not least, leaving no one behind. We cannot have two weights, two measures. We cannot have states which are not able to participate in moving ahead, in accessing finance, or in having available technology because they don't produce it themselves. I think that is my last point. Thank you.

Thank you, moderator and excellencies. Let me make short, shorter. Korea may provide one piece of practical evidence. Our plan was to have a few minutes for Q&A, but we are going to pass that in the interest of making sure that the other panelists have the time to make their presentation. Thank you so much, Chair, Excellencies, distinguished panelists, dear colleagues. Let me begin by commending Peter Thomson for convening this timely dialogue. And thank you, Dr. Rama, for the privilege to take part in this panel to speak on behalf of Portugal and the Portuguese people. In fact, Portugal and the Portuguese people have long been strong advocates of the ocean climate biodiversity nexus. This was true in 1998 when we invited the world for Expo 98 to learn about the importance of the ocean. This was true when we were updating our national ocean strategy. This was true when we signed to be founding members of the Ocean Panel. This was true when we co-hosted the UNOC 2 and marked the adoption of the Lisbon Declaration, Our Ocean, Our Future, our responsibility. And this is true today when we witness every day the perils of ignoring this nexus in our climate, in our economy, and among our people. And let me be clear, there can be no effective climate policy without an effective ocean policy. Ocean action and climate agendas must become one single exercise in governance. This means that NDCs must include the ocean, its role as a carbon sink, and as a foundation of life. As we look toward COP31, Portugal holds high expectations that the ocean will finally get the rightful central place in these negotiations, advancing to a more coherent ocean governance. Good expectations come from the momentum generated at the Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue in Bonn and the Blue Dialogue Ocean and Sea Summit in Trondheim. This momentum must now translate into real action. In Portugal, we are acting. We are steadily advancing in ocean accounts for ecosystem services so we can frame and describe our ocean areas by their natural capital. Among others, it will be possible to finally quantify carbon sequestration capacity and to map the flows of blue carbon across our national maritime spaces. In this regard, the marine protected areas we are designating can serve as a testbed for this exercise. With the forthcoming classification of the Dom Carlos Marine Nature Reserve, Portugal will be close to placing 25% of our maritime space under a protection regime. We intend to include the measurement of the benefits this protection delivers, including carbon capture in MPAs management plans and showcase it so we can bring society along. This involves turning data more transparent, and for that, we are improving our national oceanographic database, not upon the dot PT, and also pay close attention to local and traditional knowledge. Coastal communities, namely seats and traditional sea users, hold a unique understanding of the marine environmental and remain allies in policy implementation on the ground and on water. Ladies and gentlemen, As part of our mandate as non-permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, starting in January next year, we will prevent, protect and partner on oceans. Portugal stands ready to work with partners to turn the ocean climate biodiversity nexus into an agenda of implementation through 2030. By then, the question should no longer be if the ocean belongs at the center of climate action as it did in 1998. It should be if we have done enough to translate that understanding into results and those results into positive change. I thank you.

A great message to start off with your membership in the Security Council. Thank you very much, Madam Minister. Our next speaker is Dr. Peter Demenokel. He is the President and Director of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. Peter, you have the floor.

Thank you, Rana. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for the opportunity to join this important dialogue. We live on an ocean planet and we should see the ocean for what it is, this one big interconnected system, as the Prime Minister from Tonga has reminded us of. And I submit for you today that our knowledge of it should be organized this way as well. This is why ocean observing is so important, and this is really the central theme of my intervention today. As all of us know, you cannot manage what you do not measure. Observation enables prediction, prediction enables policy, policy mobilizes finance, and implementation itself must be measured again. One of the greatest examples of this, indeed one of the greatest examples of international collaboration, is something called the Argo program. About a little over 4,000 robots are in the ocean today measuring temperature and salinity and parameters of ocean health. These give us really an unprecedented view of the physical state of the upper ocean. Indeed, there are other initiatives that are being launched internationally, such as Ocean Eye and Mission Neptune, representing opportunities to enhance further still our ocean observing capability. That means observing ecosystem health at the surface, not just simply counting fish landings after the fact. We need to know where species are moving, where food webs are changing, where the whales are going, where oxygen is declining, and how a warming and acidifying ocean is affecting ocean health itself. It means observing the ocean twilight zone, this vast region of the upper kilometer in the ocean, where biomass is 100 times greater than all the surface fisheries combined. This ecosystem plays a fundamental role in the ocean carbon cycle and is key to climate regulation. And it also means observing the seabed where we're making decisions about deep sea resources and ecosystems that we have barely seen, let alone monitored through time. So the challenge is not just scientific, it's institutional and financial. On average, much less than 1% of national research budgets focus on ocean science. Yet governments are increasingly making ocean related commitments through their climate plans, biodiversity frameworks, fisheries agreements, and the BBNJ process. These commitments can't be implemented or held accountable without a sustained and sustainable ocean observing system. So let me just end with a question to keep my remarks short. What is the one thing that government should do differently by 2030 as we seek to understand this ocean climate biodiversity nexus? And my answer would be this. They should, we should fund and govern ocean observing as a permanent international public good. Because if this room represented the global ocean, the size of this room, if this was the Global ocean, the part of the ocean that we've actually observed, that we've actually been to, is the equivalent of this postage stamp. So we're looking at this most important resource of our ocean planet through the smallest of keyholes. And the first act of ocean leadership, I believe, is to open our eyes. Thank you.
Thank you very much, Peter, for that. And next speaker is Tiago Pita da Cunha, Chief Executive Officer of the Oceana Azul Foundation.

I'd like to be brief as well, and speaking about a new understanding of the ocean as the solution for where we are. Of course, we are speaking about climate, ocean, and biodiversity, which means that we are speaking about the atmosphere, where climate lies mostly, the biosphere, where the biodiversity belongs, and the hydrosphere, where the ocean is 99% of it. In Rio, it was very clear that we dealt with the atmosphere and the biosphere, but we have not dealt with the hydrosphere. The ocean was not in Rio in '92. But why did this happen? I think that the way we see the ocean was very important here. We don't see the ocean as the life support system of the planet, even the ultimate life support system of the planet, given the importance of the ocean for biosphere, for hydrosphere, and for the cryosphere. But because we probably still see the ocean with the lenses of the common paradigm of the ocean as a pool of natural resources. So that's why, of course, we have justified economic exclusive zones. And that's why we also justify territorial waters. Why? Because we also see the ocean as a space, a geographical space mostly, to a point that we don't recognize one ocean, but we declare five oceans. And that's how we teach children. So we still are in the plural, Ambassador Peter Thomson, in what relates to the ocean. We have the sound bite of one ocean, but we haven't actually interiorize the difference that the understanding of the ocean can make a difference. So in a way we know now that we need, in order to save the planet, we need to save the climate. And in order to save the climate, we need to save the ocean. But how will we save the ocean, really? Well, to start with, probably this new understanding of the ocean, not as that pool of natural resources only, not as that geographical space only, but as the complex system that took billions of years to be formed and that consists of the natural and ultimate infrastructure of our planet will change very much the way we could project things, starting with governance there. Maybe this will allow us to rethink the way we look into the mandates of UNEP CCC, the mandates of CBD, where the ocean really has no room to stay. Maybe we probably need also to consider that in order to save the planet, you need to decarbonize, but we also need to re-neutralize the planet. And that's where maybe 30x30 needs more to develop and implement its framework than what we have now in the current system of governance. So I'd say that With a new paradigm of ocean understanding, we will probably have a new paradigm for ocean governance, where the planetary dimension that comes from Rio and that's kept to the ocean can be introduced into the equation. So we have today a paradigm for climate, planet sustainability, one for biodiversity, planet sustainability, but we still do not have the framework for ocean, planet sustainability. And here I would say that 2030 is probably too soon, But that's 2040, it will probably be too late. Thank you.

Thank you, Rama, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, excellencies. We have a huge amount to celebrate in the ocean finance space, I think. The first was alluded to by Peter Thompson, Ambassador Thompson, at the beginning of the proceedings, which is 10 years ago, none of us were talking about ocean finance, except perhaps maybe a few people. And over that 10-year period, everyone's now talking about ocean finance, but quite often in a way that I think is not yet nuanced. in the way of a sophisticated discussion. And that's not surprising given the evolution of the discussion. There's no shortage of capital. We hear that a lot. And there's no shortage of implementable and investable projects. We also hear that a lot. And there's no shortage of goodwill. We hear that a lot. So what's the problem when it comes to unlocking blue finance for the projects that we need? I think part of the challenge is If we're going to make the ocean investable at a scale and at a risk and in a way that gives a return on capital, then it's less important that we persuade investors of the importance of the ocean and more important that we present investable ideas to them that meet their needs for a return. And that may be, you know, that's a nuanced argument, I think. So in the interest of time, I will pause there. With your indulgence, Raman, if I may, I'd like to ask Kushla Munro just to make a few comments as the COP31 presidency. Oh, OK, understood. I withdraw. Thank you.
Thank you.

Thank you so much, Roma. It's a pleasure to be here. In fact, so I am the executive director of the Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance, which is an alliance of 150 banks, financial institutions, insurers, governments, civil society organizations, and multilaterals. And today is our seventh birthday because we were launched at the Climate Action Summit in 2019. And at that time, there were literally four blue finance products on the market. And as Tony has just said, how things have changed. Mia Mottley, the Prime Minister of Barbados, has a wonderful quote about finance. It is the oxygen, not the destination. And I think that is key for all of us to remember as we think about the role of finance in delivering on the goals that we want to see. Initially, there was a total gap in the market. of ocean finance. But today what we're seeing is that there is a market in the gap with research indicating that there's about $550 billion per annum of potential investment into regenerative and sustainable blue economy sectors every year between now and 2030. And that includes everything from those market seeking return sectors, like offshore wind, port infrastructure, and shipping to those that are maybe not going to get those returns in terms of ocean conservation, sustainable fisheries. So we've got to think about how do we bundle some of those things together and how do we take that systemic intervention to work across the capital stack to make a difference. So again, in the interest of time, I'd like to suggest we take four steps as a community. First, and particularly as we head into COP31. Secondly, we need to move beyond our ocean bubble and look to convene finance ministers and the heads of the multilateral development banks around the table so that we can draw from the hopefully outcomes this week of the Committee on Finance that has taken place in Australia and begin to integrate ocean finance into climate finance. Thirdly, we need to take the high integrity investment principles that both prime ministers spoke to at the beginning of the session and incorporate them into the way that financing is done. We've got to address debt and credit ratings, the small sizes of tickets, and think about how we can move those things together. They are highly interested, but they need deals that fit the transaction sizes that they are looking for, and they are keen to move forward in this space. if they can see that the public sector is getting behind it and helping to move the space forward. Thank you very much.

Because if someone knows how to solve problems, it is the private sector. The first one is a clear recognition that some of the conflicts that are affecting waterways and that are affecting some of the maritime industries, of course, they come with a lot of downsides, but there have been met also with the creation of some opportunities. That comes also with an acceleration of renewable energy as people think about energy security and the disconnection from the grid that sometimes needs to happen and that renewable energy can meet the demand on. And so on and so forth, examples of opportunity within this crisis that unfortunately that has been the trigger, but that again, that creativity to build resilient businesses has actually advanced in many ways some of the agendas that we have been trying to advance just in the last 12 months. The second thing that I want to highlight as progress is that, you know, last year I heard a lot of disillusion actually on how the private sector was not only on the ocean, but in nature as a whole. And this year I hear a lot more hope. And the reason for that is that last year everything was about artificial intelligence. And it was really about how people are cost saving, how people are creating the next big model. This year, I just came from a conversation with our community of 60 plus chief sustainability officers at the World Economic Forum. And the first thing that they said was, last year, I was competing for internal allocation of capital against AI. This year, I am being used to use that capital to implement AI solutions that save us costs from a sustainability perspective. And I think there's something really profound in that. And that's something that governments should be aware of. It's the incentives that are going to take us to that exploitation of that opportunity on something that used to be as competition and now is being seen as part of the solution. And to keep it short, I had a couple of things that I wanted to say, but to keep it short, I think that we still have a lot of questions to address. We talk a lot about the cost of inaction, the return on action of these kinds of things. But I think we still need some of the deep thinking and the deep numbers. And so in the spirit of an ocean solutions dialogue, I think that the next thing that we need to do is to really partner between governments and the private sector to answer at least some of these questions. How do we better integrate nature into a strengthening project economics? And we need the real expertise for that. How do we demonstrate that healthy ecosystems protect the asset base of businesses that depend on it? How do we manage ocean exposure in a way that improves access to capital? How do we integrate considerations of community engagement to demonstrate that this has a direct return on license to operate? And how do we help with early engagement in policy processes that eventually will result in better incentives for taking action on nature and specific in the ocean. Thank you.

Thank you very much. I prepared some summary remarks. I'm going to read them very quickly, and then I'll hand it over to Ambassador Thompson to close the meeting. It's been just a remarkable two hours that we spent. We covered a great deal in a very short time. And so the main conclusions, if I could summarize them, they would probably be five. And I'll try to be very brief in saying that. And in fact, many of the conclusions, Prime Minister Teo, are drawn from your remarks. And so the first, of course, is that we cannot treat ocean any longer as a collection of separate issues. And the point that has been made by several of you here is treating that as an infrastructure issue, and then we'll come to that just in a bit. The climate change, biodiversity loss, fisheries, pollution, deep seabed, and the high seas, they're all governed through different institutions, agreements, but they operate within one connected ocean system. We heard from speaker after speaker Fragmentation is not merely an institutional inconvenience. It produces gaps, duplication, competing demands, and ultimately slower implementation. The message from this dialogue is therefore not that we need another institution. It is that existing institutions must work together, and I take that as the message from the Prime Minister of Tonga. that the United Nations system has a responsibility in conducting these processes, reduce unnecessary burdens, and translate political commitments into coordinated support. Second, the point that has been made very powerfully here is that the science must be treated as essential infrastructure for action, both Peter the Minocal and Mina Vardva talked about how we cannot manage what we do not observe, understand, and measure. Sustained ocean observation, open and usable data, scientific cooperation, and indigenous and local knowledge all contribute to our appreciation of what we need to do and are, in fact, the foundation for effective decision early warning, adaptation, conservation, and investment. Third, we must connect ambition with means of implementation. And the point that Inia has made, as well as several others, the constraint is not simply a shortage of capital. Too often, promising ocean solutions remain too small, too fragmented, are insufficiently prepared, and we must fix that. And the point that Alfredo in particular has made about the private sector, that it must be more than a source of finance. They contribute innovation, technology, data, supply chains, and delivery capacity, and we must engage how they serve public priorities, environmental integrity, et cetera. The last point I want to do is to really talk about how the dialogue and what must point forward. It takes place at an important moment, following the Pacific Islands Forum and the Trabzon Ministerial High-Level Meeting, and ahead of the pre-COP meetings in COP31 in Antalya. The task now is to carry these discussions into a coherent and durable ocean outcome at COP31, one that connects the negotiated processes, the action agenda, and complementary presidency-led initiatives. Antalya should not simply restate that ocean matters. It should show what governments and institutions will do differently, how they will strengthen coordination, support implementation, mobilize fit-for-purpose finance, expand access to science and technology, and establish accountability for delivery. If COP31 is to merit the name Blue COP, and more than anybody else, Ambassador Thompson popularized the term, the ocean must be visible not only in its narrative, but in its outcomes and the machinery of implementation that follows. We should carry this message from this room into the UN Climate Summit tomorrow, the pre-COP process in Fiji and Tuvalu, and finally Antalya. We should ask the UN system to improve the coherences across ocean-related mandates and institutions. We should turn today's proposals into specific actions with responsible actors, resources, and timelines. And we should ensure that the voices of the Pacific, small island states, coastal communities, scientists, and young people remain central throughout. Today's discussion has made one point unmistakable: there can be no climate stability without a healthy and resilient ocean, and there will be no effective ocean action without cooperation across borders, institutions, and sectors. With that, I thank you and hand over the floor back to the chair of the dialogue, Ambassador Peter Thomson.
